final_result.h1: Arcade Machine for Bar ROI: A Realistic Payback Timeline
final_result.intro:
There is a particular kind of purchase that sits awkwardly between pleasure and business. You have a bar area - in the basement, at the lake house, or in the event barn you rent out on summer weekends - and you have been looking at arcade machines. The nostalgia part of that decision is easy. The part that keeps stalling is the money: does a machine costing several thousand dollars ever earn its price back, or does it just sit in the corner looking handsome while the invoice quietly stays paid?

Search for an answer and you will find two kinds of content, neither of them much use. The first is forum guesswork, where somebody reports that a machine "does about a hundred a week" without saying what kind of venue, what price per play, or whether that hundred is gross or net. The second is vendor copy, which tends to arrive at a payback period of a few months by quietly leaving out the revenue split, the electricity, and the fact that the good weeks were summer weeks. Both give you a number. Neither gives you a way to check it.

This article takes the opposite approach. It builds three explicitly labelled scenarios - pessimistic, base case, and optimistic - states every assumption in plain sight, shows the arithmetic from weekly takings through to monthly net and payback in months, and then, separately, shows what the machine earns per month once it has paid for itself. Those are two different questions and most content blurs them into one.

One honest note before the numbers start. Every dollar figure in the scenarios below is an illustrative modelling assumption chosen so you can follow and re-run the arithmetic, not a sourced industry statistic and not a measurement of any particular machine in any particular venue. The value here is the method and the transparency of the inputs. Substitute your own numbers and the model still works.

sections.heading: Why Arcade Machine ROI Questions Deserve a Clear-Eyed Answer
sections.body_markdown:
The question "how fast does an arcade machine for a bar pay for itself?" sounds like it should have a single answer, and that is exactly why the answers you find are unreliable. A bartop machine in a busy college-town pub and the same machine in a lake house that opens twelve weekends a year are not the same investment. They are not even close. Presenting one average figure for both is not simplification, it is misinformation with a decimal point attached.

What makes the vagueness worse is that arcade profitability content is written almost entirely for people already in the amusement route business - operators who place dozens of machines and think in fleet averages. If you own one venue and are weighing one machine, fleet averages tell you nothing about your own downside. You do not get to average a bad placement against a good one. You get the placement you have.

> **[VISUAL]** *image - an unbranded bartop-style arcade machine sitting on the end of a bar counter in a quiet, warmly lit adult venue, no logos visible*

There is also a definitional problem sitting underneath most of these discussions. "ROI" gets used to mean at least three different things: the time until the purchase price is recovered, the ongoing profit after that point, and the annual rate of return on the capital tied up. They produce very different-looking numbers from the same machine. A machine that takes fourteen months to pay for itself and then nets four thousand dollars a year for the next four years is a good piece of equipment described badly if you only quote the fourteen months.

So the structure here is deliberate. First the variables that actually move the outcome. Then three scenarios with every input stated. Then the payback period. Then, as a separate output, the ongoing net profit. And at the end, a plain disclosure of what the model cannot tell you, because a numbers article that never admits its own limits is just sales copy with a table in it.

sections.heading: What Actually Drives Arcade Machine Profitability
sections.body_markdown:
Before any figure means anything, it helps to know which levers are doing the work. In practice, the payback period on a bar arcade machine is decided by five things: how many people pass the machine and are inclined to play, whether you own the venue or split takings with someone who does, how evenly that traffic is spread across the year, what you charge per play, and what the machine costs you to keep running.

Notice what is not on that list. The brand of machine, the number of games inside it, and the quality of the display matter enormously to whether people play at all - but they influence the outcome through the play-count variable, not alongside it. This is a useful thing to hold onto when you are comparing equipment. A machine that gets played twice as often is worth twice as much to you regardless of what is printed on its spec sheet, and a machine nobody touches is worth nothing however good it is.

The other thing worth saying plainly is that four of those five levers are properties of your venue, not of the machine. You can research equipment endlessly and still not know what you will earn, because the honest answer depends on a room you already know better than any vendor does. The sections below work through each lever so that when the scenarios arrive, you can see immediately which of your own assumptions is doing the heavy lifting.

sections.heading: Foot Traffic and Venue Type
sections.body_markdown:
Play counts follow dwell time more closely than they follow headcount. A venue where people stand, order, and leave within twenty minutes generates very little machine revenue no matter how many bodies move through it. A venue where people sit for two hours with a drink, in groups of three or four, with a gap between conversations - that is where a bartop machine earns. This is why quiet neighbourhood bars sometimes out-earn busier ones, and why a private event space can perform surprisingly well despite modest attendance.

The second factor is placement within the room. A machine on a back wall behind a pillar is a different asset from the same machine at the end of the bar where people waiting for drinks can see the screen. If you have ever watched somebody idly tap a screen because it was in front of them and they had ninety seconds to fill, you already understand most of what drives coin drop in a bar.

For the reader this article is really written for - somebody who hosts, and who also owns or is weighing a secondary property with a bar area - the useful comparison is not against a city pub. It is against your own calendar. If the barn hosts eighteen events a year with sixty guests each, that is roughly a thousand guest-visits. If one in eight of those guests plays twice at a dollar a play, you have a fairly firm anchor for the year without guessing at anybody's industry average. That kind of bottom-up estimate is almost always more accurate than a borrowed weekly figure, because you are the only person who actually knows your traffic.

When you build your own estimate, be conservative about the fraction who play. Interest in a new machine is high in the first weeks and settles afterwards, particularly with a regular crowd who have all seen it.

sections.heading: Revenue Split Between Bar and Machine Owner
sections.body_markdown:
This is the variable most likely to make published earnings figures useless to you, because it changes who the money belongs to and almost nobody states which side of it they are quoting from.

There are two common arrangements. In the first, you own the venue and you buy the machine outright. Every dollar dropped into it is yours, and your only ongoing outgoings are power and upkeep. In the second, a route operator owns the machine, places it in somebody else's bar, and the takings are split - a fifty-fifty division between operator and location is the arrangement most often described, and it is the one this article uses when it models the placement case. Treat that percentage as an illustrative assumption for the arithmetic, not a market standard; splits are negotiated and vary with who supplies, services, and collects.

The arithmetic consequence is blunt. Under a fifty-fifty split, the machine owner's revenue halves, and payback does not merely double - it does slightly worse than double, because collection trips and service calls do not halve along with the income. Later in this article the base case pays back in roughly twelve and a half months as an owner-operator. Modelled as a placement deal with a fifty-fifty split and twenty dollars a month allowed for collection travel, the same play rate stretches payback to somewhere near twenty-eight months.

For most readers of this piece the first arrangement applies: your venue, your machine, all of the coin drop. That is the assumption the three scenarios use, and it is stated again in the limitations section so nobody carries the wrong figure away. If you are considering putting a machine into a bar you do not own, halve every revenue number that follows before you go any further.

sections.heading: Seasonality and Slow Periods
sections.body_markdown:
A weekly revenue figure implies fifty-two of them. Very few venues get fifty-two good ones, and secondary leisure properties frequently get fewer than half that many.

This is where borrowed numbers do the most damage. Take a play rate that would be entirely reasonable during a busy stretch, annualise it across the whole year, and the payback period you calculate can be off by a factor of two. A lake house bar that is genuinely lively from May to September is not a low-earning venue - it is a normal-earning venue with a short season, and those are different problems requiring different arithmetic.

Here is that case worked all the way through, using the same base-case play rate this article settles on below. Assume the venue is in use for twenty-two weeks a year at eighty-five plays per week at one dollar a play. Gross takings are 85 x 22 = **$1,870 a year**. The machine is unplugged out of season, so electricity runs for twenty-two weeks at the $3.78 weekly figure calculated in the next section, or **$83**. Hold the maintenance reserve at the full **$120** for the year, since a machine that sits idle still ages. Net annual return is 1,870 - 83 - 120 = **$1,667**. Against a $4,250 purchase price, that is a payback of 4,250 / 1,667 = **2.55 years, or about 31 months**.

That is not a bad outcome - it is a slow one, and it is honest. If your venue is seasonal, run the annual version of the model rather than the weekly one. Weekly figures flatter seasonal properties in a way that only becomes obvious in year three.

sections.heading: Maintenance, Electricity, and the Costs Nobody Quotes
sections.body_markdown:
Gross takings are not profit, and the gap between them is where most published ROI claims quietly cheat. Two recurring costs need naming before any payback figure is credible.

Electricity first, because the question comes up constantly and the answer is reassuring. A machine left powered continuously at an assumed draw of 150 watts uses 0.15 kW x 168 hours = **25.2 kWh a week**. At an assumed residential rate of $0.15 per kilowatt-hour, that is **$3.78 a week**, roughly **$16 a month**, or about **$197 a year**. Both the wattage and the rate are placeholder assumptions for the model - substitute your own utility rate, and substitute the manufacturer's figure for whatever machine you are considering. But the order of magnitude holds: running a bartop machine around the clock is a small line item, comparable to a second refrigerator, and it is not what decides whether the investment works.

Maintenance is harder to pin down and more consequential. This model sets aside **$120 a year, or $10 a month**, as a reserve rather than a forecast - there is no reliable public figure for what a given machine will cost to keep running, and any article that quotes one precisely is guessing. What you can reason about is exposure. Machines with joysticks, buttons, and coin mechanisms have moving parts under constant contact, and those parts are the usual source of service calls. A touchscreen interface removes the controls most exposed to that kind of wear, which lowers the exposure without eliminating it - screens and power supplies can still fail, and a warranty is worth reading closely for exactly that reason.

Two further costs deserve a mention even though the model does not price them. One is your own time: emptying a cash box, reconciling takings, and dealing with the occasional fault is unpaid labour, and at low revenue levels it can exceed the profit. The other is the cost of capital - money spent on a machine is money not doing something else. Neither appears in the tables below, and both belong in your own judgement.

sections.heading: Three Payback Scenarios: Pessimistic, Base Case, and Optimistic
sections.body_markdown:
Now the numbers. Every scenario below uses the same purchase price, the same recurring costs, and the same one-dollar price per play, and varies only the number of plays per week. That is deliberate: with a single moving part, you can see exactly what drives the result and how sensitive it is.

The anchor price is **$4,250 USD**, the list price of the JVL ECHO HD3 Commercial Edition - the venue-specification machine with bill and coin acceptors fitted. It is used here because it is a real, published, checkable figure rather than a rounded-off "a machine costs about four thousand", and because a model built on an unverifiable price is not a model. It is stated as a list price and nothing more. If you are pricing a different machine, put your own figure in its place; the arithmetic does not care.

The shared assumptions across all three scenarios are: price per play $1.00; owner-operator, so no revenue split; fifty-two operating weeks a year; electricity $3.78 a week; maintenance reserve $10 a month. Monthly figures are calculated as weekly x 52 / 12, which gives 4.333 weeks per month rather than the four weeks people usually assume - a small correction that matters over a payback period.

Each scenario is labelled honestly and they are **not** equally likely. That question gets its own section after the table, because presenting three outcomes side by side without ranking their probability is one of the ways this kind of content misleads people who are trying to be careful.

sections.heading: Pessimistic Scenario Assumptions
sections.body_markdown:
The pessimistic case assumes **30 plays per week**. That is roughly four plays a day: a machine that people notice, use occasionally, and mostly walk past. It describes a low-dwell venue, a poor placement in the room, an older regular crowd with no interest, or a machine that has been in the same spot long enough that the novelty has fully worn off with a fixed clientele.

The arithmetic runs as follows. Weekly gross is 30 x $1.00 = **$30**. Monthly gross is 30 x 52 / 12 = **$130.00**. Subtract the shared recurring costs of $16.38 in electricity and $10.00 in maintenance reserve, or **$26.38**, and monthly net is **$103.62**. Payback on $4,250 is 4,250 / 103.62 = **41 months**, which is three years and five months.

Is that a disaster? It depends entirely on what you expected. As a financial investment, a three-and-a-half-year payback on a piece of equipment with a finite service life is weak - you are recovering your capital slowly and taking depreciation risk while you do it. As an amenity that happens to defray its own cost, it is perfectly respectable; the room has something in it that guests enjoy, and over four years it costs you nothing net.

What this scenario really tells you is where the floor sits. Even at four plays a day, the machine is not losing money in the operating sense - the recurring costs are low enough that almost any level of use covers them. The risk in a low-traffic venue is not ongoing loss. It is capital sitting still, which is a different and more forgivable problem.

sections.heading: Base Case Scenario Assumptions
sections.body_markdown:
The base case assumes **85 plays per week**, or about twelve a day. This is the scenario to plan around, and it is chosen to describe an ordinary outcome rather than a good one: a venue with reasonable dwell time, sensible placement where people can see the screen, a mixed crowd, and normal weekly variation between quiet Mondays and busy Saturdays.

Weekly gross is 85 x $1.00 = **$85**. Monthly gross is 85 x 52 / 12 = **$368.33**. Subtract the same **$26.38** in recurring costs and monthly net is **$341.95**. Payback on $4,250 is 4,250 / 341.95 = **12.4 months** - call it twelve to thirteen months, and call it fourteen if you want a margin for the weeks you have not thought of.

A year to recover the purchase price is, in my view, a genuinely sound result for a capital item of this kind, and it is the figure I would build a decision on. It is slow enough to be believable and fast enough to justify the outlay without heroic assumptions about your customers. It also has a useful property: the play rate would have to fall by more than half before payback stretched past three years. That is a wide margin of safety, and margin of safety is what you want from a first-time equipment purchase.

The pressure test worth running is the per-play price. At $0.50 a play instead of $1.00, the base case halves to roughly $171 net a month and payback stretches to about twenty-five months. Pricing is the one lever you fully control, and it moves the outcome as much as traffic does.

sections.heading: Optimistic Scenario Assumptions
sections.body_markdown:
The optimistic case assumes **175 plays per week**, or twenty-five a day. This is a strong result and it requires several things to go right at once: high dwell time, a sociable crowd that plays in pairs, a prominent position, and either a busy year-round venue or an event schedule dense enough to substitute for one.

Weekly gross is 175 x $1.00 = **$175**. Monthly gross is 175 x 52 / 12 = **$758.33**. Less the same **$26.38** in recurring costs, monthly net is **$731.95**. Payback on $4,250 is 4,250 / 731.95 = **5.8 months** - under six months, which is the sort of figure vendor copy likes to quote as typical.

It is not typical. It is what a well-placed machine in a genuinely well-suited venue can do, and the reason to include it is not to raise your expectations but to define the ceiling honestly. If a page tells you a machine pays for itself in five months, you now know roughly what has to be true for that claim to hold, and you can ask whether it is true of your room.

One caution about the optimistic case specifically: high play rates are the most likely to decay. A machine drawing twenty-five plays a day is being played hard, often by the same regulars, and the novelty curve is steeper the harder it starts. If your first two months look like this scenario, resist the temptation to annualise them. Wait for month six before you decide what the machine actually earns.

sections.heading: Comparison Table: Weekly Revenue and Payback Period by Scenario
sections.body_markdown:
Here are the three scenarios side by side. Every figure traces back to the assumptions stated above: $1.00 per play, owner-operator with no revenue split, 52 operating weeks, $3.78 a week in electricity, $10 a month in maintenance reserve, and a $4,250 purchase price. Monthly figures use 4.333 weeks per month.

| Scenario | Plays / week | Weekly gross | Monthly net | Payback |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pessimistic | 30 | $30 | $103.62 | 41 months |
| Base case | 85 | $85 | $341.95 | 12.4 months |
| Optimistic | 175 | $175 | $731.95 | 5.8 months |

> **[VISUAL]** *chart - simple horizontal bar chart comparing payback period in months across the three scenarios, base case visually emphasised*

The spread is the point. A machine in a slow room and the same machine in a busy one differ by a factor of seven in payback time, which is why a single published average is worse than useless - it is precise enough to be trusted and wrong for almost everybody.

Two variants are worth holding alongside the table. If your venue is seasonal at twenty-two weeks a year, the base case play rate produces roughly **31 months** rather than 12.4, as worked through earlier. If the machine is placed in a bar you do not own on a fifty-fifty split, with twenty dollars a month allowed for collection trips, the base case stretches to roughly **28 months**. Neither of those is in the table because they change the structure of the deal rather than one input, and mixing them in would make the comparison dishonest.

If you want to sanity-check any row, the sequence is: plays x price = weekly gross; weekly gross x 52 / 12 = monthly gross; monthly gross - $26.38 = monthly net; $4,250 / monthly net = months to payback. Every number above survives that check.

sections.heading: Which Scenario Should You Actually Plan Around?
sections.body_markdown:
The three scenarios are not equally probable, and treating them as if they were is the single most common way this analysis goes wrong. My view is straightforward: plan around the base case, treat the pessimistic case as your risk test, and treat the optimistic case as an upside you do not budget for.

The reason is not that the base case is statistically demonstrated - none of these figures are, and the limitations section says so plainly. It is that the base case is the only one built on assumptions that do not require anything unusual. It assumes a machine people can see, a room where people linger, and a normal mix of good and quiet weeks. The optimistic case requires several favourable conditions to hold simultaneously and to keep holding, which is a much stronger claim about the future than most venue owners can honestly make about their own trade.

There is also a decay effect that none of the scenarios model, and it argues for conservatism. Play rates in a venue with a stable, regular customer base typically start high and settle, because the people who were going to try it have tried it. In a venue with high turnover - a resort bar, a rented event space, somewhere with new faces every week - the decay is much weaker, because the novelty is renewed by the audience rather than by the machine. If your crowd is the same forty people, weight your estimate downward. If your crowd changes constantly, the flat assumption in these scenarios is closer to fair.

As a planning benchmark, here is what I would use. A payback inside **eighteen months** is a good outcome for equipment of this kind and justifies the purchase on financial grounds alone. **Eighteen to thirty-six months** is acceptable if the machine also does something for the room - and it usually does, because a machine people enjoy keeps them at the bar longer, which shows up in drink sales rather than coin drop. Beyond **thirty-six months**, be honest with yourself: you are buying an amenity that partly defrays its own cost, not making an investment. That can still be the right decision. It is just a different one, and it deserves to be made with open eyes.

sections.heading: Net Monthly Profit After Payback: What Happens Next
sections.body_markdown:
Payback is where most articles stop, and it is the less interesting half of the question. Once the purchase price is recovered, the recurring costs are all that stand between the coin drop and your pocket - and those costs are small. The machine does not get more expensive to run because it has finished paying for itself.

From month thirteen onward in the base case, the same $341.95 monthly net that was retiring the purchase price becomes profit. Annualised, that is 341.95 x 12 = **$4,103 a year**. Against the $4,250 originally committed, that works out to an annual return of about **96%** on the capital - not because the machine is remarkable, but because equipment with low running costs and no consumables behaves that way once it is paid off.

| Scenario | Monthly net | Annual net (year 2+) | Return on $4,250 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pessimistic | $103.62 | $1,243 | ~29% |
| Base case | $341.95 | $4,103 | ~96% |
| Optimistic | $731.95 | $8,783 | ~207% |

> **[VISUAL]** *chart - cumulative cash flow line for the base case over 36 months, showing the crossover point at month 12-13 where the line passes zero*

Those percentages need reading carefully rather than enthusiastically. They are returns on the purchase price only. They do not account for depreciation - the machine is worth less each year and will eventually need replacing - nor for your own unpaid time collecting and reconciling cash, nor for the risk that a major component fails outside warranty. A three-figure percentage on a spreadsheet always looks better than the same outcome described as "about four thousand dollars a year from a four-thousand-dollar machine, before my time and before it wears out".

The more useful way to hold it is this. In the base case, the machine costs you money for a year, then contributes roughly the price of a second machine every year thereafter. In the pessimistic case, it costs you money for three and a half years and then contributes modestly. In neither case does it lose money on an operating basis once installed, because $26 a month of running cost is a very low bar to clear. That asymmetry - limited ongoing downside, meaningful ongoing upside - is the actual argument for the purchase, and it is stronger and more honest than any payback figure quoted on its own.

sections.heading: How This Model Was Built: Using a Real List Price to Run Your Own Numbers
sections.body_markdown:
The method here is deliberately plain, and the only genuinely fixed input is the price. Everything else is an assumption you should replace.

The $4,250 anchor is the published list price of the JVL ECHO HD3 Commercial Edition, the venue-configuration machine with bill and coin acceptors. It was chosen because a model needs one number that a sceptical reader can independently check, and "roughly four thousand dollars" is not that number. It is stated as a list price, plainly, and it is not a promotion or an offer of any kind. If you are pricing different equipment, swap the figure in and every downstream result recalculates.

To run the model on your own venue, work through it in this order:

1. **Estimate plays per week from the bottom up.** Count guest-visits per week, estimate the fraction who will play, and estimate plays each. Do not borrow somebody else's weekly dollar figure - you know your room and they do not.
2. **Multiply by your price per play** to get weekly gross. This is the single biggest lever you directly control.
3. **Convert to monthly correctly:** weekly gross x 52 / 12. Using four weeks per month understates the year by about 8%.
4. **Apply your revenue split if the venue is not yours.** Halve the figure for a fifty-fifty placement, then subtract collection costs.
5. **Subtract electricity:** (watts / 1000) x hours per week x your kWh rate. Use the manufacturer's stated draw and your own utility bill.
6. **Subtract a maintenance reserve.** A hundred to a hundred and fifty dollars a year is a reasonable placeholder until you have real service history.
7. **Divide the purchase price by monthly net** to get payback in months - then re-run the whole thing at 60% of your play estimate and see whether you can still live with the answer.

That last step is the one people skip and the one that matters most. A model that only works under your best guess is not a model, it is a hope. If step seven still produces a number you find acceptable, you have a decision you can defend. If it does not, the machine may still be worth buying - but as an amenity, priced accordingly, and not as an investment case.

sections.heading: Where the JVL ECHO Fits Into This Picture
sections.body_markdown:
Since the model is anchored to a specific price, it is only fair to say what that price buys and, more importantly, which version of it applies to which situation - because the distinction is one that a lot of vendor content leaves deliberately blurry.

There are two editions, and they are not interchangeable. The **JVL ECHO HD3 Commercial Edition** is the venue machine: it includes a bill acceptor taking $1, $5, $10, and $20 notes with a 500-bill capacity, and a coin acceptor for quarters. It is intended for bars, restaurants, and operators, and its list price is **$4,250 USD**. That is the machine every revenue figure in this article refers to. The **JVL ECHO HD3 Home Edition** is a free-play machine with no bill validator and no coin acceptor, intended for residential use, at a list price of **$3,990 USD**. It cannot take money, so none of the payback arithmetic above applies to it in any form. If your bar area is in your basement and you are not charging anyone, that is the one you want, and the [Echo for Home overview](https://jvl.ca/en/home) is the right place to start.

A few things in the specification bear directly on the cost side of the model rather than the revenue side. The controls are touchscreen rather than joysticks and buttons, which removes the components most exposed to mechanical wear - not a guarantee against failure, but a smaller surface of things that wear out. The case is reinforced plastic on a precision-built frame, designed for the kind of handling bar environments produce. All 149 games are pre-installed and the machine runs fully offline, so there is no connectivity charge, no subscription, and no download to fail on a Friday night. And the machine ships with a 1-Year All-Inclusive Manufacturer Warranty, with JVL covering shipping both ways for warranty service, which is worth noting as a first-year cost-of-ownership floor rather than a maintenance estimate.

> **[VISUAL]** *image - close-up of the JVL ECHO Commercial Edition bill and coin acceptor area, showing the note slot and coin mech in a bar setting*

On the reliability assumptions the model quietly depends on, the production process is worth a sentence. Physical assembly of a unit takes hours once components have passed incoming inspection, but the full cycle to a shippable unit can run up to seven working days - configuration, manual and automated testing, burn-in, a second QC pass, and packing. Every unit is powered on and tested individually before it leaves the factory, covering system boot, the touchscreen across its whole surface, image, sound, game loading, controls, power, and the swivel mechanism at minimum. The machines are designed in Canada and made in the USA, and the format itself is not new: JVL has been building bartop machines since 1995 and the ECHO is the eleventh generation of that line. JVL bartops have been awarded "Best Bartop Video Game of the Year" by RePlay Magazine multiple times - a record belonging to the bartop line as a whole rather than to this model specifically.

If the arithmetic above has you at the point of checking specifications rather than concepts, the [JVL ECHO product page](https://jvl.ca/en/echo) has the full detail on both editions. Read it the way you would read any equipment sheet: against your own numbers, not instead of them.

sections.heading: Assumptions and Limitations
sections.body_markdown:
This section exists because the article would not deserve trust without it. Everything modelled above is arithmetic built on stated assumptions, and here is exactly what those assumptions are and where they are weakest.

- **All revenue figures are illustrative modelling inputs.** The play counts of 30, 85, and 175 per week, the $1.00 price per play, and the fifty-fifty placement split were chosen to make the arithmetic transparent and re-runnable. They are not sourced industry statistics, not survey results, and not measurements of any machine in any venue.
- **The electricity figure is a placeholder.** The model assumes a 150-watt continuous draw at $0.15 per kWh. Neither figure is confirmed for any specific machine or region. Use the manufacturer's stated consumption and your own utility rate.
- **The maintenance reserve is a reserve, not a forecast.** $120 a year is a planning placeholder. No verified service-call frequency or repair-cost data underpins it.
- **No decay, depreciation, or cost of capital is modelled.** Play rates are held flat across the payback window, the machine's residual value is ignored, and no interest or opportunity cost is charged against the $4,250.
- **Your own time is unpriced.** Cash collection, reconciliation, and dealing with faults are real labour costs that the model does not subtract.

Two further boundaries are worth stating. The scenarios assume you own both the venue and the machine and therefore keep all takings; if that is not your arrangement, every revenue figure needs adjusting before it means anything. And the whole analysis applies to a machine that can take payment - the free-play home configuration generates no revenue by design, and no part of this model should be read as suggesting otherwise.

What you should take away is not a payback number. It is a method: estimate plays from your own traffic, convert honestly to monthly, subtract the costs by name, divide by the real purchase price, and then run it again at sixty percent to see what your downside actually looks like. If the answer still works at sixty percent, you have something you can decide on. That is a more useful thing to own than any figure somebody else calculated for a venue that was not yours.

# Arcade Machine for Bar ROI: A Realistic Payback Timeline

There is a particular kind of purchase that sits awkwardly between pleasure and business. You have a bar area - in the basement, at the lake house, or in the event barn you rent out on summer weekends - and you have been looking at arcade machines. The nostalgia part of that decision is easy. The part that keeps stalling is the money: does a machine costing several thousand dollars ever earn its price back, or does it just sit in the corner looking handsome while the invoice quietly stays paid?

Search for an answer and you will find two kinds of content, neither of them much use. The first is forum guesswork, where somebody reports that a machine "does about a hundred a week" without saying what kind of venue, what price per play, or whether that hundred is gross or net. The second is vendor copy, which tends to arrive at a payback period of a few months by quietly leaving out the revenue split, the electricity, and the fact that the good weeks were summer weeks. Both give you a number. Neither gives you a way to check it.

This article takes the opposite approach. It builds three explicitly labelled scenarios - pessimistic, base case, and optimistic - states every assumption in plain sight, shows the arithmetic from weekly takings through to monthly net and payback in months, and then, separately, shows what the machine earns per month once it has paid for itself. Those are two different questions and most content blurs them into one.

One honest note before the numbers start. Every dollar figure in the scenarios below is an illustrative modelling assumption chosen so you can follow and re-run the arithmetic, not a sourced industry statistic and not a measurement of any particular machine in any particular venue. The value here is the method and the transparency of the inputs. Substitute your own numbers and the model still works.

## Why Arcade Machine ROI Questions Deserve a Clear-Eyed Answer

The question "how fast does an arcade machine for a bar pay for itself?" sounds like it should have a single answer, and that is exactly why the answers you find are unreliable. A bartop machine in a busy college-town pub and the same machine in a lake house that opens twelve weekends a year are not the same investment. They are not even close. Presenting one average figure for both is not simplification, it is misinformation with a decimal point attached.

What makes the vagueness worse is that arcade profitability content is written almost entirely for people already in the amusement route business - operators who place dozens of machines and think in fleet averages. If you own one venue and are weighing one machine, fleet averages tell you nothing about your own downside. You do not get to average a bad placement against a good one. You get the placement you have.

> **[VISUAL]** *image - an unbranded bartop-style arcade machine sitting on the end of a bar counter in a quiet, warmly lit adult venue, no logos visible*

There is also a definitional problem sitting underneath most of these discussions. "ROI" gets used to mean at least three different things: the time until the purchase price is recovered, the ongoing profit after that point, and the annual rate of return on the capital tied up. They produce very different-looking numbers from the same machine. A machine that takes fourteen months to pay for itself and then nets four thousand dollars a year for the next four years is a good piece of equipment described badly if you only quote the fourteen months.

So the structure here is deliberate. First the variables that actually move the outcome. Then three scenarios with every input stated. Then the payback period. Then, as a separate output, the ongoing net profit. And at the end, a plain disclosure of what the model cannot tell you, because a numbers article that never admits its own limits is just sales copy with a table in it.

## What Actually Drives Arcade Machine Profitability

Before any figure means anything, it helps to know which levers are doing the work. In practice, the payback period on a bar arcade machine is decided by five things: how many people pass the machine and are inclined to play, whether you own the venue or split takings with someone who does, how evenly that traffic is spread across the year, what you charge per play, and what the machine costs you to keep running.

Notice what is not on that list. The brand of machine, the number of games inside it, and the quality of the display matter enormously to whether people play at all - but they influence the outcome through the play-count variable, not alongside it. This is a useful thing to hold onto when you are comparing equipment. A machine that gets played twice as often is worth twice as much to you regardless of what is printed on its spec sheet, and a machine nobody touches is worth nothing however good it is.

The other thing worth saying plainly is that four of those five levers are properties of your venue, not of the machine. You can research equipment endlessly and still not know what you will earn, because the honest answer depends on a room you already know better than any vendor does. The sections below work through each lever so that when the scenarios arrive, you can see immediately which of your own assumptions is doing the heavy lifting.

### Foot Traffic and Venue Type

Play counts follow dwell time more closely than they follow headcount. A venue where people stand, order, and leave within twenty minutes generates very little machine revenue no matter how many bodies move through it. A venue where people sit for two hours with a drink, in groups of three or four, with a gap between conversations - that is where a bartop machine earns. This is why quiet neighbourhood bars sometimes out-earn busier ones, and why a private event space can perform surprisingly well despite modest attendance.

The second factor is placement within the room. A machine on a back wall behind a pillar is a different asset from the same machine at the end of the bar where people waiting for drinks can see the screen. If you have ever watched somebody idly tap a screen because it was in front of them and they had ninety seconds to fill, you already understand most of what drives coin drop in a bar.

For the reader this article is really written for - somebody who hosts, and who also owns or is weighing a secondary property with a bar area - the useful comparison is not against a city pub. It is against your own calendar. If the barn hosts eighteen events a year with sixty guests each, that is roughly a thousand guest-visits. If one in eight of those guests plays twice at a dollar a play, you have a fairly firm anchor for the year without guessing at anybody's industry average. That kind of bottom-up estimate is almost always more accurate than a borrowed weekly figure, because you are the only person who actually knows your traffic.

When you build your own estimate, be conservative about the fraction who play. Interest in a new machine is high in the first weeks and settles afterwards, particularly with a regular crowd who have all seen it.

### Revenue Split Between Bar and Machine Owner

This is the variable most likely to make published earnings figures useless to you, because it changes who the money belongs to and almost nobody states which side of it they are quoting from.

There are two common arrangements. In the first, you own the venue and you buy the machine outright. Every dollar dropped into it is yours, and your only ongoing outgoings are power and upkeep. In the second, a route operator owns the machine, places it in somebody else's bar, and the takings are split - a fifty-fifty division between operator and location is the arrangement most often described, and it is the one this article uses when it models the placement case. Treat that percentage as an illustrative assumption for the arithmetic, not a market standard; splits are negotiated and vary with who supplies, services, and collects.

The arithmetic consequence is blunt. Under a fifty-fifty split, the machine owner's revenue halves, and payback does not merely double - it does slightly worse than double, because collection trips and service calls do not halve along with the income. Later in this article the base case pays back in roughly twelve and a half months as an owner-operator. Modelled as a placement deal with a fifty-fifty split and twenty dollars a month allowed for collection travel, the same play rate stretches payback to somewhere near twenty-eight months.

For most readers of this piece the first arrangement applies: your venue, your machine, all of the coin drop. That is the assumption the three scenarios use, and it is stated again in the limitations section so nobody carries the wrong figure away. If you are considering putting a machine into a bar you do not own, halve every revenue number that follows before you go any further.

### Seasonality and Slow Periods

A weekly revenue figure implies fifty-two of them. Very few venues get fifty-two good ones, and secondary leisure properties frequently get fewer than half that many.

This is where borrowed numbers do the most damage. Take a play rate that would be entirely reasonable during a busy stretch, annualise it across the whole year, and the payback period you calculate can be off by a factor of two. A lake house bar that is genuinely lively from May to September is not a low-earning venue - it is a normal-earning venue with a short season, and those are different problems requiring different arithmetic.

Here is that case worked all the way through, using the same base-case play rate this article settles on below. Assume the venue is in use for twenty-two weeks a year at eighty-five plays per week at one dollar a play. Gross takings are 85 x 22 = **$1,870 a year**. The machine is unplugged out of season, so electricity runs for twenty-two weeks at the $3.78 weekly figure calculated in the next section, or **$83**. Hold the maintenance reserve at the full **$120** for the year, since a machine that sits idle still ages. Net annual return is 1,870 - 83 - 120 = **$1,667**. Against a $4,250 purchase price, that is a payback of 4,250 / 1,667 = **2.55 years, or about 31 months**.

That is not a bad outcome - it is a slow one, and it is honest. If your venue is seasonal, run the annual version of the model rather than the weekly one. Weekly figures flatter seasonal properties in a way that only becomes obvious in year three.

### Maintenance, Electricity, and the Costs Nobody Quotes

Gross takings are not profit, and the gap between them is where most published ROI claims quietly cheat. Two recurring costs need naming before any payback figure is credible.

Electricity first, because the question comes up constantly and the answer is reassuring. A machine left powered continuously at an assumed draw of 150 watts uses 0.15 kW x 168 hours = **25.2 kWh a week**. At an assumed residential rate of $0.15 per kilowatt-hour, that is **$3.78 a week**, roughly **$16 a month**, or about **$197 a year**. Both the wattage and the rate are placeholder assumptions for the model - substitute your own utility rate, and substitute the manufacturer's figure for whatever machine you are considering. But the order of magnitude holds: running a bartop machine around the clock is a small line item, comparable to a second refrigerator, and it is not what decides whether the investment works.

Maintenance is harder to pin down and more consequential. This model sets aside **$120 a year, or $10 a month**, as a reserve rather than a forecast - there is no reliable public figure for what a given machine will cost to keep running, and any article that quotes one precisely is guessing. What you can reason about is exposure. Machines with joysticks, buttons, and coin mechanisms have moving parts under constant contact, and those parts are the usual source of service calls. A touchscreen interface removes the controls most exposed to that kind of wear, which lowers the exposure without eliminating it - screens and power supplies can still fail, and a warranty is worth reading closely for exactly that reason.

Two further costs deserve a mention even though the model does not price them. One is your own time: emptying a cash box, reconciling takings, and dealing with the occasional fault is unpaid labour, and at low revenue levels it can exceed the profit. The other is the cost of capital - money spent on a machine is money not doing something else. Neither appears in the tables below, and both belong in your own judgement.

## Three Payback Scenarios: Pessimistic, Base Case, and Optimistic

Now the numbers. Every scenario below uses the same purchase price, the same recurring costs, and the same one-dollar price per play, and varies only the number of plays per week. That is deliberate: with a single moving part, you can see exactly what drives the result and how sensitive it is.

The anchor price is **$4,250 USD**, the list price of the JVL ECHO HD3 Commercial Edition - the venue-specification machine with bill and coin acceptors fitted. It is used here because it is a real, published, checkable figure rather than a rounded-off "a machine costs about four thousand", and because a model built on an unverifiable price is not a model. It is stated as a list price and nothing more. If you are pricing a different machine, put your own figure in its place; the arithmetic does not care.

The shared assumptions across all three scenarios are: price per play $1.00; owner-operator, so no revenue split; fifty-two operating weeks a year; electricity $3.78 a week; maintenance reserve $10 a month. Monthly figures are calculated as weekly x 52 / 12, which gives 4.333 weeks per month rather than the four weeks people usually assume - a small correction that matters over a payback period.

Each scenario is labelled honestly and they are **not** equally likely. That question gets its own section after the table, because presenting three outcomes side by side without ranking their probability is one of the ways this kind of content misleads people who are trying to be careful.

### Pessimistic Scenario Assumptions

The pessimistic case assumes **30 plays per week**. That is roughly four plays a day: a machine that people notice, use occasionally, and mostly walk past. It describes a low-dwell venue, a poor placement in the room, an older regular crowd with no interest, or a machine that has been in the same spot long enough that the novelty has fully worn off with a fixed clientele.

The arithmetic runs as follows. Weekly gross is 30 x $1.00 = **$30**. Monthly gross is 30 x 52 / 12 = **$130.00**. Subtract the shared recurring costs of $16.38 in electricity and $10.00 in maintenance reserve, or **$26.38**, and monthly net is **$103.62**. Payback on $4,250 is 4,250 / 103.62 = **41 months**, which is three years and five months.

Is that a disaster? It depends entirely on what you expected. As a financial investment, a three-and-a-half-year payback on a piece of equipment with a finite service life is weak - you are recovering your capital slowly and taking depreciation risk while you do it. As an amenity that happens to defray its own cost, it is perfectly respectable; the room has something in it that guests enjoy, and over four years it costs you nothing net.

What this scenario really tells you is where the floor sits. Even at four plays a day, the machine is not losing money in the operating sense - the recurring costs are low enough that almost any level of use covers them. The risk in a low-traffic venue is not ongoing loss. It is capital sitting still, which is a different and more forgivable problem.

### Base Case Scenario Assumptions

The base case assumes **85 plays per week**, or about twelve a day. This is the scenario to plan around, and it is chosen to describe an ordinary outcome rather than a good one: a venue with reasonable dwell time, sensible placement where people can see the screen, a mixed crowd, and normal weekly variation between quiet Mondays and busy Saturdays.

Weekly gross is 85 x $1.00 = **$85**. Monthly gross is 85 x 52 / 12 = **$368.33**. Subtract the same **$26.38** in recurring costs and monthly net is **$341.95**. Payback on $4,250 is 4,250 / 341.95 = **12.4 months** - call it twelve to thirteen months, and call it fourteen if you want a margin for the weeks you have not thought of.

A year to recover the purchase price is, in my view, a genuinely sound result for a capital item of this kind, and it is the figure I would build a decision on. It is slow enough to be believable and fast enough to justify the outlay without heroic assumptions about your customers. It also has a useful property: the play rate would have to fall by more than half before payback stretched past three years. That is a wide margin of safety, and margin of safety is what you want from a first-time equipment purchase.

The pressure test worth running is the per-play price. At $0.50 a play instead of $1.00, the base case halves to roughly $171 net a month and payback stretches to about twenty-five months. Pricing is the one lever you fully control, and it moves the outcome as much as traffic does.

### Optimistic Scenario Assumptions

The optimistic case assumes **175 plays per week**, or twenty-five a day. This is a strong result and it requires several things to go right at once: high dwell time, a sociable crowd that plays in pairs, a prominent position, and either a busy year-round venue or an event schedule dense enough to substitute for one.

Weekly gross is 175 x $1.00 = **$175**. Monthly gross is 175 x 52 / 12 = **$758.33**. Less the same **$26.38** in recurring costs, monthly net is **$731.95**. Payback on $4,250 is 4,250 / 731.95 = **5.8 months** - under six months, which is the sort of figure vendor copy likes to quote as typical.

It is not typical. It is what a well-placed machine in a genuinely well-suited venue can do, and the reason to include it is not to raise your expectations but to define the ceiling honestly. If a page tells you a machine pays for itself in five months, you now know roughly what has to be true for that claim to hold, and you can ask whether it is true of your room.

One caution about the optimistic case specifically: high play rates are the most likely to decay. A machine drawing twenty-five plays a day is being played hard, often by the same regulars, and the novelty curve is steeper the harder it starts. If your first two months look like this scenario, resist the temptation to annualise them. Wait for month six before you decide what the machine actually earns.

## Comparison Table: Weekly Revenue and Payback Period by Scenario

Here are the three scenarios side by side. Every figure traces back to the assumptions stated above: $1.00 per play, owner-operator with no revenue split, 52 operating weeks, $3.78 a week in electricity, $10 a month in maintenance reserve, and a $4,250 purchase price. Monthly figures use 4.333 weeks per month.

| Scenario | Plays / week | Weekly gross | Monthly net | Payback |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pessimistic | 30 | $30 | $103.62 | 41 months |
| Base case | 85 | $85 | $341.95 | 12.4 months |
| Optimistic | 175 | $175 | $731.95 | 5.8 months |

> **[VISUAL]** *chart - simple horizontal bar chart comparing payback period in months across the three scenarios, base case visually emphasised*

The spread is the point. A machine in a slow room and the same machine in a busy one differ by a factor of seven in payback time, which is why a single published average is worse than useless - it is precise enough to be trusted and wrong for almost everybody.

Two variants are worth holding alongside the table. If your venue is seasonal at twenty-two weeks a year, the base case play rate produces roughly **31 months** rather than 12.4, as worked through earlier. If the machine is placed in a bar you do not own on a fifty-fifty split, with twenty dollars a month allowed for collection trips, the base case stretches to roughly **28 months**. Neither of those is in the table because they change the structure of the deal rather than one input, and mixing them in would make the comparison dishonest.

If you want to sanity-check any row, the sequence is: plays x price = weekly gross; weekly gross x 52 / 12 = monthly gross; monthly gross - $26.38 = monthly net; $4,250 / monthly net = months to payback. Every number above survives that check.

## Which Scenario Should You Actually Plan Around?

The three scenarios are not equally probable, and treating them as if they were is the single most common way this analysis goes wrong. My view is straightforward: plan around the base case, treat the pessimistic case as your risk test, and treat the optimistic case as an upside you do not budget for.

The reason is not that the base case is statistically demonstrated - none of these figures are, and the limitations section says so plainly. It is that the base case is the only one built on assumptions that do not require anything unusual. It assumes a machine people can see, a room where people linger, and a normal mix of good and quiet weeks. The optimistic case requires several favourable conditions to hold simultaneously and to keep holding, which is a much stronger claim about the future than most venue owners can honestly make about their own trade.

There is also a decay effect that none of the scenarios model, and it argues for conservatism. Play rates in a venue with a stable, regular customer base typically start high and settle, because the people who were going to try it have tried it. In a venue with high turnover - a resort bar, a rented event space, somewhere with new faces every week - the decay is much weaker, because the novelty is renewed by the audience rather than by the machine. If your crowd is the same forty people, weight your estimate downward. If your crowd changes constantly, the flat assumption in these scenarios is closer to fair.

As a planning benchmark, here is what I would use. A payback inside **eighteen months** is a good outcome for equipment of this kind and justifies the purchase on financial grounds alone. **Eighteen to thirty-six months** is acceptable if the machine also does something for the room - and it usually does, because a machine people enjoy keeps them at the bar longer, which shows up in drink sales rather than coin drop. Beyond **thirty-six months**, be honest with yourself: you are buying an amenity that partly defrays its own cost, not making an investment. That can still be the right decision. It is just a different one, and it deserves to be made with open eyes.

## Net Monthly Profit After Payback: What Happens Next

Payback is where most articles stop, and it is the less interesting half of the question. Once the purchase price is recovered, the recurring costs are all that stand between the coin drop and your pocket - and those costs are small. The machine does not get more expensive to run because it has finished paying for itself.

From month thirteen onward in the base case, the same $341.95 monthly net that was retiring the purchase price becomes profit. Annualised, that is 341.95 x 12 = **$4,103 a year**. Against the $4,250 originally committed, that works out to an annual return of about **96%** on the capital - not because the machine is remarkable, but because equipment with low running costs and no consumables behaves that way once it is paid off.

| Scenario | Monthly net | Annual net (year 2+) | Return on $4,250 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pessimistic | $103.62 | $1,243 | ~29% |
| Base case | $341.95 | $4,103 | ~96% |
| Optimistic | $731.95 | $8,783 | ~207% |

> **[VISUAL]** *chart - cumulative cash flow line for the base case over 36 months, showing the crossover point at month 12-13 where the line passes zero*

Those percentages need reading carefully rather than enthusiastically. They are returns on the purchase price only. They do not account for depreciation - the machine is worth less each year and will eventually need replacing - nor for your own unpaid time collecting and reconciling cash, nor for the risk that a major component fails outside warranty. A three-figure percentage on a spreadsheet always looks better than the same outcome described as "about four thousand dollars a year from a four-thousand-dollar machine, before my time and before it wears out".

The more useful way to hold it is this. In the base case, the machine costs you money for a year, then contributes roughly the price of a second machine every year thereafter. In the pessimistic case, it costs you money for three and a half years and then contributes modestly. In neither case does it lose money on an operating basis once installed, because $26 a month of running cost is a very low bar to clear. That asymmetry - limited ongoing downside, meaningful ongoing upside - is the actual argument for the purchase, and it is stronger and more honest than any payback figure quoted on its own.

## How This Model Was Built: Using a Real List Price to Run Your Own Numbers

The method here is deliberately plain, and the only genuinely fixed input is the price. Everything else is an assumption you should replace.

The $4,250 anchor is the published list price of the JVL ECHO HD3 Commercial Edition, the venue-configuration machine with bill and coin acceptors. It was chosen because a model needs one number that a sceptical reader can independently check, and "roughly four thousand dollars" is not that number. It is stated as a list price, plainly, and it is not a promotion or an offer of any kind. If you are pricing different equipment, swap the figure in and every downstream result recalculates.

To run the model on your own venue, work through it in this order:

1. **Estimate plays per week from the bottom up.** Count guest-visits per week, estimate the fraction who will play, and estimate plays each. Do not borrow somebody else's weekly dollar figure - you know your room and they do not.
2. **Multiply by your price per play** to get weekly gross. This is the single biggest lever you directly control.
3. **Convert to monthly correctly:** weekly gross x 52 / 12. Using four weeks per month understates the year by about 8%.
4. **Apply your revenue split if the venue is not yours.** Halve the figure for a fifty-fifty placement, then subtract collection costs.
5. **Subtract electricity:** (watts / 1000) x hours per week x your kWh rate. Use the manufacturer's stated draw and your own utility bill.
6. **Subtract a maintenance reserve.** A hundred to a hundred and fifty dollars a year is a reasonable placeholder until you have real service history.
7. **Divide the purchase price by monthly net** to get payback in months - then re-run the whole thing at 60% of your play estimate and see whether you can still live with the answer.

That last step is the one people skip and the one that matters most. A model that only works under your best guess is not a model, it is a hope. If step seven still produces a number you find acceptable, you have a decision you can defend. If it does not, the machine may still be worth buying - but as an amenity, priced accordingly, and not as an investment case.

## Where the JVL ECHO Fits Into This Picture

Since the model is anchored to a specific price, it is only fair to say what that price buys and, more importantly, which version of it applies to which situation - because the distinction is one that a lot of vendor content leaves deliberately blurry.

There are two editions, and they are not interchangeable. The **JVL ECHO HD3 Commercial Edition** is the venue machine: it includes a bill acceptor taking $1, $5, $10, and $20 notes with a 500-bill capacity, and a coin acceptor for quarters. It is intended for bars, restaurants, and operators, and its list price is **$4,250 USD**. That is the machine every revenue figure in this article refers to. The **JVL ECHO HD3 Home Edition** is a free-play machine with no bill validator and no coin acceptor, intended for residential use, at a list price of **$3,990 USD**. It cannot take money, so none of the payback arithmetic above applies to it in any form. If your bar area is in your basement and you are not charging anyone, that is the one you want, and the [Echo for Home overview](https://jvl.ca/en/home) is the right place to start.

A few things in the specification bear directly on the cost side of the model rather than the revenue side. The controls are touchscreen rather than joysticks and buttons, which removes the components most exposed to mechanical wear - not a guarantee against failure, but a smaller surface of things that wear out. The case is reinforced plastic on a precision-built frame, designed for the kind of handling bar environments produce. All 149 games are pre-installed and the machine runs fully offline, so there is no connectivity charge, no subscription, and no download to fail on a Friday night. And the machine ships with a 1-Year All-Inclusive Manufacturer Warranty, with JVL covering shipping both ways for warranty service, which is worth noting as a first-year cost-of-ownership floor rather than a maintenance estimate.

> **[VISUAL]** *image - close-up of the JVL ECHO Commercial Edition bill and coin acceptor area, showing the note slot and coin mech in a bar setting*

On the reliability assumptions the model quietly depends on, the production process is worth a sentence. Physical assembly of a unit takes hours once components have passed incoming inspection, but the full cycle to a shippable unit can run up to seven working days - configuration, manual and automated testing, burn-in, a second QC pass, and packing. Every unit is powered on and tested individually before it leaves the factory, covering system boot, the touchscreen across its whole surface, image, sound, game loading, controls, power, and the swivel mechanism at minimum. The machines are designed in Canada and made in the USA, and the format itself is not new: JVL has been building bartop machines since 1995 and the ECHO is the eleventh generation of that line. JVL bartops have been awarded "Best Bartop Video Game of the Year" by RePlay Magazine multiple times - a record belonging to the bartop line as a whole rather than to this model specifically.

If the arithmetic above has you at the point of checking specifications rather than concepts, the [JVL ECHO product page](https://jvl.ca/en/echo) has the full detail on both editions. Read it the way you would read any equipment sheet: against your own numbers, not instead of them.

## Assumptions and Limitations

This section exists because the article would not deserve trust without it. Everything modelled above is arithmetic built on stated assumptions, and here is exactly what those assumptions are and where they are weakest.

- **All revenue figures are illustrative modelling inputs.** The play counts of 30, 85, and 175 per week, the $1.00 price per play, and the fifty-fifty placement split were chosen to make the arithmetic transparent and re-runnable. They are not sourced industry statistics, not survey results, and not measurements of any machine in any venue.
- **The electricity figure is a placeholder.** The model assumes a 150-watt continuous draw at $0.15 per kWh. Neither figure is confirmed for any specific machine or region. Use the manufacturer's stated consumption and your own utility rate.
- **The maintenance reserve is a reserve, not a forecast.** $120 a year is a planning placeholder. No verified service-call frequency or repair-cost data underpins it.
- **No decay, depreciation, or cost of capital is modelled.** Play rates are held flat across the payback window, the machine's residual value is ignored, and no interest or opportunity cost is charged against the $4,250.
- **Your own time is unpriced.** Cash collection, reconciliation, and dealing with faults are real labour costs that the model does not subtract.

Two further boundaries are worth stating. The scenarios assume you own both the venue and the machine and therefore keep all takings; if that is not your arrangement, every revenue figure needs adjusting before it means anything. And the whole analysis applies to a machine that can take payment - the free-play home configuration generates no revenue by design, and no part of this model should be read as suggesting otherwise.

What you should take away is not a payback number. It is a method: estimate plays from your own traffic, convert honestly to monthly, subtract the costs by name, divide by the real purchase price, and then run it again at sixty percent to see what your downside actually looks like. If the answer still works at sixty percent, you have something you can decide on. That is a more useful thing to own than any figure somebody else calculated for a venue that was not yours.
